item.title: Adaptive attention routing multimodal expert graph neural network for drug-drug interaction prediction
item.description: arXiv:2611.33200v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate prediction of drug-drug interactions (DDIs) is essential for drug safety in combination therapy. Multimodal methods built on knowledge graphs (KGs) already combine molecular structures, substructures, targets and biomedical relations into drug representations, but they still face three problems: features are heterogeneous across modalities, fusion does not adapt to individual drug pairs, and modality-specific information is diluted during integration. We propose the adaptive attention routing multimodal expert graph neural network (AARME-GNN) to address them. A Feature Adaptive Calibration Module (FACM) reduces within-modality noise in each representation through bottleneck reparameterization and channelwise recalibration before fusion. A Multimodal Weight Router (MMWR) then sets the modality weights of each drug pair, with an entropy constraint that prevents the weights from collapsing onto one modality. A Routing-Aware Weighted Distillation (RAWD) mechanism builds a soft target from the unimodal branches, so that the fusion classifier retains the knowledge held by each modality. On Dataset 1, AARME-GNN improves precision over MKG-FENN by 3.71 and 6.57 percentage points in known drug and known new drug prediction, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) by 4.53 in new drug prediction. On Dataset 2, the advantage is concentrated in the two cold-start settings and in precision.
item.dc:creator: Jingyi Yang, Chengcheng Yan, Hongri Cong, Feifei Zhao

item.title: Using waveform types, discrete Sobolev distances, and trend compatibility to cluster short time series of clinical data
item.description: arXiv:2611.33623v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clinical tests, such as the oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), perturb a physiological system at rest and record its excursion over a fixed protocol window as a short, undersampled time series. Such curves rarely allow parameter identification at the individual level, yet their trends carry physiological information that emerges at the population level as recurrent response patterns. Standard clustering methods aggregate differences globally and average out those trends, losing precisely the information about how the system regains control after the perturbation; identifying response patterns requires a method that preserves them. We present a nonparametric framework that factorizes each curve into unit waveforms, sorts them with a symbolic trend-compatibility filter, and compares compatible shapes using discrete Sobolev-type distances on finite differences up to order $k$. The number of clusters, i.e., distinct response types, equals the number of realizable trend patterns the cohort populates, validated by resampling. Applied to 1283 five-point OGTTs, the method identifies 7 glycemia and 8 insulinemia types. The count holds across a threefold range of resolution. In benchmarks against six classical clustering methods, ours alone never mixes opposite trends, with comparable reconstruction error and stability. Clinical normality, assessed after clustering, is graded, overlapping, and distributed unevenly across response types ($h=0.14$--$0.48$). Overall, our method distinguishes response types among curves too short for alignment-based methods yet too informative for reduction to summary values. It applies to any protocol recording a system's response to a standardized perturbation on a short grid.
item.dc:creator: Robyn J. N. Kettlitz, Daniel Cisternas, Alvaro Olivera-Nappa, David Medina-Ortiz, Seba Contreras

item.title: Milk-removal feedback shapes lactation sustainability and daily output in a model of human lactation
item.description: arXiv:2611.33997v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Milk production during lactation is dynamically regulated by milk removal, yet quantitative models linking feeding or pumping schedules to subsequent production remain scarce. We develop a minimal model describing milk accumulation and production between removal sessions, and the stimulation of subsequent production through milk removal. We compare different assumptions about how stimulation depends on the amount of milk removed or the duration of removal, and consider two removal protocols: prescribing either the removed amount or the removal duration. When stimulation depends on the removed amount, declining production can reduce subsequent stimulation and reinforce the decline. This leads to a critical wait interval beyond which no repeated constant schedule can sustain lactation. If stimulation is inefficient for small removal amounts but more efficient at intermediate amounts, the model can exhibit bistability: depending on the initial conditions, milk production either persists or ceases. In contrast, duration-dependent stimulation does not permit a zero-production state under continued removal, but can generate non-constant long-term dynamics under certain conditions. We further show that maximizing milk removal per session need not maximize daily output, because increased removal competes with session frequency. The framework provides a basis for testing alternative feedback hypotheses against longitudinal data and for optimizing feeding and pumping schedules.
item.dc:creator: Angelika Manhart, Tobias M\"uller

item.title: Resolving cell states in spatial transcriptomics with SCATTER
item.description: arXiv:2611.34798v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A capture spot can contain transcripts from multiple cell types. Differences between spots may reflect changes in cell-type proportions, expression within a cell type, or both, making local cell-type expression difficult to infer from mixed counts. We developed SCATTER to estimate cell-type proportions and relative expression profiles for each cell type at each spot from spatial transcriptomic counts, coordinates, and annotated single-cell reference data. SCATTER weights reference cell profiles using local spatial context, then jointly fits the resulting profiles and cell-type proportions to reconstruct spot counts. Cell2location estimates regularize the proportions. After fitting, SCATTER uses learned gene-specific calibration factors and fitted proportions to allocate observed counts among cell types. In five pseudo-spot benchmarks constructed from imaging data, SCATTER achieved higher cross-spot correlations with measured expression for 82.8-99.8% of evaluated gene-cell type pairs in pairwise comparisons with DestVI, PANDA, and STged. In breast cancer Xenium data, it recovered gene expression associated with the tumor neighborhood and regulon scores. In breast cancer Visium data, inferred stromal and macrophage expression showed distinct associations with neighborhood malignant cell proportions. In multiple sclerosis brain tissue, SCATTER recovered lesion-associated glial expression programs. In colorectal cancer Visium HD data, it mapped cell-type-specific programs at the invasive front and ranked candidate ligand-receptor pairs. SCATTER enables analysis of spatial expression variation within cell types from mixed tissue measurements.
item.dc:creator: Lei Huang, Yun Gong, Weiqiang Lin, Lindong Jiang, Hui Shen, Chaoyang Zhang, Hong-Wen Deng

item.title: DDxBasis: Explaining Frozen Foundation Encoder-based Medical Classification by Exact Differential Diagnosis
item.description: arXiv:2611.33358v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In differential diagnosis (DDx), a clinician explains a diagnosis by the few findings that separate it from the alternatives. Medical image classifiers cannot yet explain themselves this way. Existing explanations are either faithful but spread over hundreds of concepts, or compact but leave part of each decision unexplained. We present DDxBasis, which explains a classifier on a frozen foundation encoder as a differential diagnosis in three steps. First, a concept bottleneck reads all patch tokens at every encoder layer using gated, second-order slot attention. A concept basis then regroups the concepts into two-pole axes, each a differential between groups of diagnoses. Finally, we read a differential diagnosis from each axis through the typical presentation of its poles, the pertinent findings of the case, and counterfactual edits of borderline cases. Across five medical datasets, DDxBasis is the most accurate frozen-encoder model and close to the best published domain-specific results. Because every concept adds its own evidence, its reproducible concept basis splits each decision exactly, at no cost in accuracy. Without ordered stage or concept labels, the axes recover cell lineages and rare subtypes, agree with dermatologists' structure annotations, and expose planted and real shortcuts.
item.dc:creator: Luojie Huang, Gregory N. McKay, Nicholas J. Durr

item.title: Systematic study of the performance of small robots on controlled laboratory substrates
item.description: arXiv:2611.33702v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The design of robots able to locomote effectively over a diversity of terrain requires detailed ground interaction models; unfortunately such models are lacking due to the complicated response of real world substrates which can yield and flow in response to loading. To advance our understanding of the relevant modeling and design issues, we conduct a comparative study of the performance of DASH and RoACH, two small, biologically inspired, six legged, lightweight (10 cm, 20 g) robots fabricated using the smart composite microstructure (SCM) process. We systematically examine performance of both robots on rigid and flowing substrates. Varying both ground properties and limb stride frequency, we investigate average speed, mean mechanical power and cost of transport, and stability. We find that robot performance and stability is sensitive to the physics of ground interaction: on hard ground kinetic energy must be managed to prevent yaw, pitch, and roll instability to maintain high performance, while on sand the fluidizing interaction leads to increased cost of transport and lower running speeds. We also observe that the characteristic limb morphology and kinematics of each robot result in distinct differences in their abilities to traverse different terrains. Our systematic studies are the first step toward developing models of interaction of limbs with complex terrain as well as developing improved limb morphologies and control strategies.
item.dc:creator: Chen Li, Aaron M. Hoover, Paul Birkmeyer, Paul B. Umbanhowar, Ronald S. Fearing, Daniel I. Goldman

item.title: Exclusion and internal structure in the association/dissociation kinetics of DNA-binding proteins in the fast diffusion limit
item.description: arXiv:2611.33740v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In many canonical biophysical and biochemical contexts, complex diffusing DNA-binding proteins undergoing nonspecific adsorption and desorption can exist in different conformational states. Equilibrium binding theories and kinetic models of competing ligands provide a basis for describing these systems. Coupling the internal conformational kinetics of bound proteins to exclusion and diffusion requires tracking both protein positions and binding states. Closed-form, tractable mathematical models that accurately describe the stochastic dynamics of structured proteins that bind to and diffuse along DNA are lacking. Here, we develop a new coarse-grained stochastic model of nonspecific DNA-protein binding in the fast diffusion regime, from which we derive an effective Markov model and its corresponding mean-field approximation that incorporates protein footprint size and conformational switching. We fit our new model quantitatively to previously measured dynamics of Replication Protein A (RPA) binding to ssDNA. Finally, by including multisegment binding states, our analysis captures facilitated exchange, revealing how multisegment architecture balances high affinity with rapid remodeling. Our theoretical model applies broadly to many other DNA-binding protein systems, including nucleosomes, ssDNA-binding proteins, and other multisegment complexes, providing accurate predictions and new strategies for evaluating experimental data.
item.dc:creator: Xiangting Li, Tom Chou

item.title: Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao Reconstruction of Discrete space Population Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.33923v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reconstructing the continuous time dynamics of cell state evolution from sparse snapshot observations can be formulated as an unbalanced optimal transport problem. To study such dynamics at a coarse grained cell type level, unbalanced optimal transport must be extended to discrete state spaces. Inspired by discrete flow matching, we extended the dynamic Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao (WFR) problem to discrete spaces, and derived a closed form for its solution. For particularly large state spaces or more general models, we proposed an unbalanced discrete flow matching as a numerical approximation method, which provides a Markovian reconstruction of the optimal WFR flow. Our discrete WFR framework also stays stable across different coarse grain resolution. Finally, numerical experiments demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed approach, and applications to real biological data supported the plausibility of the reconstructed dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Junda Ying, Xinyu Wang, Peijie Zhou, Lei Zhang

item.title: Cell-Type-Specific Expression Is Hard to Predict from Bulk, but It Is Still Useful
item.description: arXiv:2611.34166v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Single-cell-informed deconvolution provides cell-type-resolved features for clinical bulk RNA cohorts. Most existing methods predict the proportions $\pi_k$ of the $K$ constituent cell types (CTs). Fewer predict cell-type-specific expression (CTSE) $\mu_{kg}$ of gene $g$ in CT $k$, which can capture cell states that proportions miss, but recent benchmarks find it much harder. We explain this gap with closed-form accuracy bounds. For CTSE, we derive an $R^2$ ceiling for per-gene linear estimators. For proportions, the best linear estimator, which pools evidence across genes, has a closed-form $R^2$, and a computable lower bound on it predicts which CTs are learnable. We study targeted deconvolution of 106 biologically curated (CT, gene) pairs, found post hoc to have higher learnability scores. On overall survival in non-small cell lung cancer, estimation difficulty does not predict prognostic value across these targets. Yet a sparse survival model on deconvolved features, mostly CTSE, predicts survival as well as a sparse model on the bulk genes themselves, while attributing its signal to specific cell types. Some deconvolved CTSE features reveal prognostic signal not seen in the corresponding bulk gene.
item.dc:creator: Gadi Naveh, Amit Miller, Gal Keinan

item.title: Did the Model Forecast It, or Already Know It? Evaluating Large Language Models for Novel Drug-Target Prioritisation with a Temporal Knowledge-Graph Oracle
item.description: arXiv:2611.34247v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI systems increasingly help decide which drug targets enter costly clinical trials. We recast each target-disease hypothesis as a dated event, the pair's first clinical trial. This lets us test whether a language model can forecast such events after its training cutoff, rather than recall events before it. We rebuild a dated biomedical knowledge graph as it stood at the end of each year from 2020 up to its newest version. We then ask six open language models, with and without this graph, which targets will enter a first trial for a disease the next year. Without retrieval, the models rank about as well as trial history, a count of each target's past trials in the same therapeutic area, also after their training cutoffs. Evidence dated before the decision adds at most a small gain, before or after the models' training cutoffs. The newest graph raises five of six models clearly above that baseline, but its paths usually include the answer: the pair's own trial, dated after the decision. Evaluations of target prioritisation should date both features and labels, with evidence from before the decision and outcomes after it.
item.dc:creator: Pui Chung Siu, Yuan Liang, Claudia Cabrera, Mani Mudaliar, Arkaitz Zubiaga

item.title: Stochastic Failure Dynamics in a Model Peptidoglycan Mesh under Hydrolysis and Mechanical Loading
item.description: arXiv:2611.34610v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop a minimal stochastic-mechanical model for failure dynamics of the Gram-negative peptidoglycan (PG) cell wall under blocked growth and continued hydrolysis. The cell wall is modelled as a collection of load-bearing cross-sections, with random number of cross-links in each such cross-section, around a fixed degree of cross-linking. To understand failure dynamics of the cell wall under antibacterial agents which prevent insertion of fresh PG material, peptide bonds are progressively excised by hydrolases, while insertion/formation of new bonds is blocked. We compare and contrast rupture dynamics in no-load and load-activated regimes, using extreme value theory and stochastic simulations, deriving limiting laws for system failure in both the long-cell and large crosslinking limits. For a cross-section with many bonds, the mean failure time grows only log- arithmically with bond number, giving diminishing returns from additional cross-linking. In the no-load case, the centered failure time converges to a Gumbel law, though crucially, load changes the centered distribution and accelerates the final stages of collapse. In long cells, failure follows a weakest-link Weibull-type scaling controlled by the least cross-linked regions, with mechanical load reducing the failure-time scale without changing the weakest-link exponent. The fraction of bonds removed before failure tends to zero, showing that collapse can remain highly localized even while the global cross-linking degree stays high. Slowing down growth and other cellular functions is a typical antibiotic escape mechanism for bacteria and in this context, we show that, hydrolase down-regulation uniformly rescales the failure-time distribution and delays collapse, but does not remove the load-induced preference for rupture in weakened regions.
item.dc:creator: Issan Patri, Garima Rani

item.title: Patterns in Individual Blood Count Trajectories in the UK Biobank Characterise Disease-Specific Signatures and May Anticipate Pan-Cancer Risk
item.description: arXiv:2604.11824v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Routine blood tests are typically interpreted as individual measurements against population-derived reference ranges, with limited use of information contained in changes across repeated tests. Here, we investigate whether trends in routinely measured haematological markers can reveal patterns associated with ageing and disease progression across cancers, cardiovascular diseases and infections. Using retrospective Complete Blood Count (CBC) data from the UK Biobank, we examine changes in individual biomarkers and their relationships across successive measurements, while assessing potential confounding factors. We combine statistical analysis, machine learning and network-based approaches to identify patterns associated with different disease states and stages. We find that clinically relevant information is contained not only in absolute blood-cell counts, but also in the direction, magnitude and coordinated patterns of change between measurements. These patterns provide candidate disease signatures that may complement conventional interpretation based on individual values and reference intervals. Because the approach relies on inexpensive tests already collected routinely in clinical practice, it offers a practical route for extracting additional clinical information from existing data, with potential applications in earlier disease detection, monitoring and precision healthcare.
item.dc:creator: Riya Nagar, Abicumaran Uthamacumaran, Adelaide de Vecchi, Hector Zenil

item.title: Can Tabular In-Context Learners Generalize to Biomolecular Property Prediction?
item.description: arXiv:2606.31126v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Predicting biomolecular properties from limited labeled data is a central bottleneck in protein engineering and small-molecule design. As strong pretrained encoders now supply rich fixed-length representations, the difficulty has shifted from representation learning to building a data-efficient predictor for the few-shot regime. Tabular foundation models such as TabPFN and TabICL perform this prediction through in-context inference after pretraining on synthetic tables. We test whether they can act as flexible interpolators over informative fixed biomolecular representations. Treating each method as a predictor-representation pair, we evaluate across two domains. On ProteinGym, TabPFN3-ESMC600M is competitive with leading supervised-substitution entries and obtains the lowest MSE among the leaderboard-context rows considered, while Kermut remains stronger by Spearman. Performance is substantially lower under modulo and contiguous holdouts than under random splits. On the five-endpoint PpEST dataset, tabular models show favorable descriptive performance against matched supervised baselines, but the random split measures within-family interpolation and the small endpoint count precludes strong model-ordering claims. For small-molecule classification with ECFP/RDKit descriptors, no single predictor-representation pairing dominates across TDC ADMET, MoleculeNet, FS-Mol, and DrugOOD, but several pairings are competitive with strong descriptor and graph baselines. Crucially, on both protein and small-molecule few-shot tasks, these predictor-representation pairs offer strong performance. We conclude that tabular foundation models can be strong biomolecular predictors, but only when coupled with expressive representations.
item.dc:creator: Davy Guan, Lu Zhang, Asiri Wijesinghe, Allen Zhu, He Zhao, Helen Power, F. Hafna Ahmed, Andrew Warden, Cheng Soon Ong, Daniel M. Steinberg

item.title: Neuromorphic architectures as numerical solvers for computational neuroscience
item.description: arXiv:2608.28387v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Neuromorphic computing is closely associated with spiking neuronal networks. However, an alternative class of so-called "rate-based" models arising from computational neuroscience and machine learning forgoes spiking interactions and instead relies on continuous coupling between neurons. Existing neuromorphic implementations designed around spike-based interactions are not well-suited for emulating such models. Here we view the distributed simulation of these models as message-passing algorithms on parallel hardware. Leveraging prior art in numerical algorithms and distributed simulation, we outline steps that enable the design of efficient digital neuromorphic accelerators for non-spiking neuronal models. In particular, we show that multi-bit packets, rather than spikes, are the most efficient communication strategy in packet-switched networks and that compared to basic numerical integration methods, higher-order differential equation solvers decrease both computation and communication costs while achieving lower numerical error, but that these benefits are ultimately limited by arithmetic precision. Using our proposed design principles, we convert an existing neuromorphic architecture into a distributed numerical solver - a spikeless neuromorphic system - for continuously-coupled neuronal models. We thereby demonstrate that our theoretical considerations indeed translate into practical advantages, namely reduced energy consumption and delay.
item.dc:creator: Jakob Jordan, Ole Richter, Congyang Li, Mihai A. Petrovici, Rajit Manohar

item.title: Functional nestedness of soil nematode communities across Europe: integrating morphological counts and eDNA reads
item.description: arXiv:2611.18819v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: 1. Soil nematodes occupy multiple trophic positions and contribute to key processes in soil food webs. Their communities vary across land uses and environmental conditions, yet it remains unclear whether these differences mainly reflect taxon replacement or nested patterns of taxon occurrence. 2. Here, we analysed two independent European datasets of soil nematode communities, SOB4ES, based on eDNA metabarcoding, and NemEu, based on morphological identification, to examine how genus composition varies across land uses. We partitioned community dissimilarity into turnover and nestedness-resultant components and compared sites under contrasting land uses with those sharing the same land use, while accounting for geographical and soil-related variation. We also assessed matrix-level nestedness, differences among trophic groups and associations between genus composition and environmental gradients. 3. In both datasets, genus turnover was consistently greater between contrasting land uses than within the same land use. Although the differences were modest, they remained significant after accounting for geographical distance and genus richness, whereas nestedness-resultant dissimilarity contributed little to land-use differentiation. These findings suggest that land-use-associated differences in European nematode communities are expressed primarily through changes in genus identity rather than nested patterns of taxon occurrence. 4. The consistency of this result across independently assembled datasets supports the broader relevance of taxonomic turnover for understanding soil biodiversity patterns across European land uses.
item.dc:creator: Giuseppe Nicolosi, Michael Bonkowski, Carlo Febbi, Christian Mulder

item.title: Lattice models of chiral random motion: A short review
item.description: arXiv:2611.32743v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Chirality, a systematic rotational bias, is ubiquitous in many random motion patterns, from bacteria cells, that swim in circles near surfaces and spinning colloids, to charged particles diffusing under the influence of magnetic fields. In two dimensions, chirality renders random transport \textit{odd}: the diffusion tensor acquires an antisymmetric part that leaves the mean-squared displacement invariant but modifies fluxes and boundary currents. Lattice models for random motion are a natural setting to study chirality, since they are exactly solvable, connect directly to heterogeneous media, cellular automata, and programmable robots, and in discrete time admit fully chiral limits with a localised bulk and edge transport. Lattice walks with a rotational bias have been introduced in different communities several times since 1960, yet without a common language or conceptual connection between them. Here we review these models from the perspective that on the lattice, chirality requires memory. Taking the recently introduced chiral random walk model as a template, we describe the walker with an internal degree of freedom. With a chiral biased updating rule, the full diffusion tensor of this chiral walker turns odd. Within this picture, we can unite persistent and chiral walks, run-and-tumble motion, and cyclic random motions in one framework. We discuss how the memory is followed into the environment; in Lorentz lattice gases, kinetic and rotor walks, and random odd environments; and into the path; in spiral self-avoiding walks.
item.dc:creator: E. Kalz, J. Wojcik, J. Uhlig, N. Sherf, Y. Roichman, R. Metzler
